correctness.rationale: For fixed \(\alpha>0\), every target prime exceeds \(\sqrt n\) for large \(n\), so Legendre's formula gives exactly \(v_p(n!)=\lfloor n/p\rfloor\). The valuation cells are precisely \(n/(j+1)<p\le n/j\). Intersecting each with \(\alpha n<p\le\beta n\) yields a finite exact \(\vartheta\)-difference decomposition, and \(\vartheta(nx)=nx+o(n)\) at the finitely many fixed positive endpoints proves the coefficient. The aligned-window and parity consequences are algebraic simplifications of that coefficient. Finite exact-cell replay agrees in 250 cases and is corroborative rather than foundational.

originality.rationale: The inspected motivating source treats the same weighted observable on fixed power bands but explicitly does not assert endpoint-uniformity. Its \(o(n\log n)\) remainder does not resolve an \(O(n)\) linear-window main term. Older residue-distribution papers fix the prime index while \(n\) varies. Targeted statement, alias, implication, and data searches located no source giving the displayed linear-window coefficient or the persistent parity bias.
residual_risks: The linear-window formula follows from classical Legendre and prime-number-theorem ingredients, so an equivalent elementary corollary could exist under terminology not surfaced by the targeted searches. No such source was located, and the closest recent paper explicitly leaves moving-endpoint uniformity outside its claim.

value.rationale: The claim addresses the first unresolved boundary scale adjacent to a new fixed-power-band equidistribution theorem. It gives a complete explicit coefficient on every fixed linear window, not a single arbitrary numerical slice, and the \(3/5\) versus \(2/5\) parity split is a structural counterexample to naive uniform continuation. The formula also identifies the harmonic valuation-cell mechanism responsible for the transition.
